newsitem.title: DENMARK: SAS braces for Scandinavian sky wars.
newsitem.headline: SAS braces for Scandinavian sky wars.

text.p: Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) vowed on Friday to fight hard to defend its dominant position in Scandinavian air traffic, as other carriers invade its home territory.
"The Copenhagen-Stockholm-Oslo triangle are vital routes for SAS, we are going to fight to the last," SAS spokesman Jens Peter Skaarup told Reuters.
On Thursday Danish airline Maersk Air announced the launch of regular flights between Copenhagen and Stockholm, the latest of several challenges to SAS rule of the region's airspace.
"We intend to fight for the routes and we are going to give nothing away to our competitors without a struggle, " he said.
Maersk, owned by shipping and energy group A.P. Moeller, said it would start the new service on April 28, in cooperation with Finland's Finnair.

"Obviously we expect that the increased competition is going to cost us money. But we are prepared and intend to meet it by offering lower priced tickets and improving our airport service just as we did with the Oslo-Stockholm route when we got competition," Skaarup added.
Norwegian group Braathens SAFE last November launched regular flights between Oslo and Stockholm, one of SAS' most profitable routes, and plans further expansion.
The Norwegian firm, which shares a frequent-flyer programme with British Airways, has bought half of Swedish domestic airline Transwede and intends to acquire the rest.
Competition is tough on the Oslo-Stockholm route and Braathens admits it has got off to difficult start with load factors at only 25 percent, half that needed for a profitable operation.
"But we are investing in the future," Braathens information chief Audun Tjomsland told the Danish financial daily Borsen.
Analysts estimate that prices on the route have fallen by 15 percent since Braathens challenged SAS, costing the latter an estimated 150 million crowns.
The Copenhagen-Stockholm route, where SAS had a virtual monopoly before deregulation, is another of the most lucrative for the airline, with about one million passengers per year.
"The route is mainly transit with many customers going on from Copenhagen to other destinations," Skaarup said.
"SAS has still a great advantage in that many of them will find it most convenient to fly on with the same airline," he added.
Analysts estimate that SAS could lose at least 100 million crowns annually from competition on the Copenhagen-Stockholm route, with ticket prices falling by several hundred crowns.

Other airlines pressing for their share of the Scandinavian pie include Danish short-haul outfit Sun-Air,which took on BA colours last May as a holder of the British Airways Express franchise, offering flights from Copenhagen and Aarhus to Oslo, Gothenburg and Stockholm.
Part of the BA Express strategy is to grab feeder traffic from SAS by slotting into BA's worldwide network for onward flights.

Aviation insiders have said that BA appeared to be positioning itself for a major assault on SAS. Maersk itself is linked to the British giant through its British-based Maersk Air Ltd., which is also a British Airways Express franchisee.

One of BA's major rivals, British tycoon Richard Branson's Virgin Express started flights between Copenhagen and its Brussels base last autumn and is openly eyeing the Copenhagen-Oslo-Stockholm triangle.
